claims.text: Spin-polarized density functional theory can be used to detect ferromagnetic ground states.
Ferromagnetic ground states can be identified by comparing the total energies of different spin configurations.
The material is initially nominally paramagnetic or non-magnetic based on its crystal structure and electron configuration.
The calculations should use spin polarization and an appropriate exchange-correlation functional.
The calculations are conducted at 0 K without an external magnetic field.
Sufficient k-point sampling and energy cutoff are needed to resolve subtle energy differences.
The crystal lattice and atomic arrangement mediate exchange interactions between electrons.
Including spin degrees of freedom permits energy comparisons among ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic, and non-magnetic configurations.
A lower total energy for the ferromagnetic configuration indicates spontaneous spin alignment driven by exchange interactions.
The spin-polarized DFT simulation will yield a lower total energy for the ferromagnetic state than for the alternative states.
Energy differences between spin configurations are negligible in known non-ferromagnetic materials.
Standard DFT may be inadequate for strongly correlated electron systems.
Standard DFT approximations may fail to capture strong electron-electron interactions accurately.
No direct supporting evidence is present in the supplied records.
The effectiveness of the method for a specific material remains uncertain without system-specific validation.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome unconditionally states that the ferromagnetic state will have lower energy, whereas the uncertainty field says effectiveness for any specific system is uncertain without validation.
